overview: The file consists of three Department of State list-of-papers or index sheets summarizing records from 1940–1941 on Japanese press controls. The indexed materials describe increasingly severe censorship of foreign correspondents’ outgoing dispatches, surveillance of liberal ideas, the scarcity of independent political commentary in the Japanese press, suppression of reporting on negotiations with the Axis powers, statutory control of news publications, hostile press treatment of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and restrictions on information bulletins issued by foreign missions. The underlying telegrams, despatches, memoranda, translations, and enclosures are referenced but are not reproduced in these three pages.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Grew report on censorship of foreign correspondents
subfiles.about: An index entry summarizes Grew’s January 15, 1940 report on the widening disparity between domestic press freedom and censorship of foreign correspondents’ outgoing dispatches.
subfiles.summary: This Department of State form records item 32, a summary of Japan Telegram 21 from Grew. It reports that the domestic press had become increasingly unrestrained while foreign correspondents’ dispatches to their home offices were being drastically cut. Grew warned that reports from Tokyo appearing in the American press might consequently fail to convey an adequate picture of Japanese conditions and developments, citing the New York Herald Tribune correspondent as an example. The entry points to sheet 5 and notes a filing reference to 811.91294.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, sheet 5: Japanese censorship measures in 1940
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes four 1940 records concerning institutional censorship, press bans, restrictions on foreign reporting, and surveillance of liberal expression.
subfiles.summary: The first entry reports indications that a projected Cabinet Intelligence Bureau would impose stricter censorship and notes an unusual lack of political articles and independent editorials in the vernacular press. A second entry concerns press bans on speculation about an extraordinary Cabinet meeting and Japanese negotiations with the Axis powers. Hornbeck’s memorandum, drawing on information from Major George F. Eliot and the New York Herald Tribune’s Tokyo correspondent, states that almost no news could leave Japan beyond official communiqués and recommends consulting Mr. Fletcher. The final entry indexes a Grew despatch on censorship and surveillance of potentially liberal ideas, accompanied by translations of illustrative Japanese newspaper articles.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, page 6: News control and anti-Roosevelt publicity in 1941
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes four 1941 records on Japan’s news-control law, disparaging coverage of Roosevelt, and restrictions on foreign missions’ publications.
subfiles.summary: One entry records Grew’s transmission of a translation of Law No. 37 of January 11 concerning control of news publications in Japan. Another references a report of disparaging Chinese-language commentary by a Japanese Army organ on President Roosevelt’s press-conference statement about the Far East. A further Grew despatch encloses an unfavorable Roosevelt cartoon from the Japan Times and Advertiser and a memorandum of conversation with its editor, Mr. Toshi Go. The last entry reports that the Japanese government would prohibit foreign missions in Tokyo from publicly circulating bulletins and other releases, prompting a British protest.

interest: These sheets are useful because they reconstruct the contents and chronology of records that are not themselves present in the surviving extract. They show that censorship operated through several overlapping mechanisms: cutting foreign correspondents’ cables, narrowing domestic political discussion, enforcing press bans, monitoring liberal expression, legislating control of news publications, and preventing foreign missions from circulating information. The entries also preserve references to otherwise difficult-to-trace enclosures—including newspaper translations, an anti-Roosevelt cartoon, and a memorandum with a Japanese editor—and document the State Department’s concern that American readers were receiving an increasingly incomplete picture of wartime Japan.
